title: The little crab and Justice
sentences: A fairy tale by Windekind.
On the sandy shore two stone breakwaters jut into the sea.
They are groins, built from great black stones.
When the tide is in and the sea has risen to its highest,
the water covers them almost entirely; at ebb they lie dry.
There sat a man on the black stones as far out into the sea as he could,
so that the water lapped around him on every side.
He looked out over the rolling water; it was still and warm.
The waves were small and came in slowly—they scarcely troubled
to curl for a moment—and then, plop!
they fell spent upon the flat beach.
Between the stones of the groin the dark-green seaweed waited patiently for the rising water.
Some formed a thick velvety carpet; the larger spread their flat,
brownish leaves abroad—waiting for the sea that would soon come.
Slowly, slowly the water rose.
With every wave it washed a little farther over the stones and hurried through the crevices and grooves; on the retreat it left airy white
foam behind with great bubbles that, one by one, burst splashing in the air.
And gratefully the seaweed lifted itself up,
when the water reached it and made the leathery leaves swell and gleam again after hours of drought.
Countless little sea creatures still lived among the weed.
Mussels held their shells firmly closed until the sea should come, and in the water
that from the previous flood had lingered in hollows between the stones, little shrimps and crabs hid—all waiting for the rising tide.
Before the feet of the solitary man lay a small dead jellyfish.
The waves had cast it half alive upon the stones, and then the sun had killed it altogether.
Its slimy, translucent body had shrivelled and grown dull.
The man bent forward to look at the strange creature.
It was still fair, bluish in colour, translucent as a gem,
and on the hemispherical back brown stripes were drawn in the shape of a star.
Yes, it had been a beautiful little jellyfish when it swam in the great sea.
But now it was dead and nothing more than a round patch of bluish slime,
that the returning sea would never bring back to life.
Then a small grey crab came thoughtfully creeping from the dark crevice between two stones.
He had sat waiting there patiently for long hours—but now the water must come soon,
he thought, and he ventured slowly and cautiously in little steps from his hiding-place.
For he had seen the dead jellyfish lying for a long time before the entrance of his hole,
and dead jellyfish is the daintiest fare that a young crab can imagine.
Slowly he scurried on over the thick carpet of green weed,
soft as moss in the forest—one two, one two, slantwise toward the jellyfish.
After every four steps he paused briefly to collect his thoughts.
The man who sat there on the stones
looked far across the rolling waves toward the great sun sinking at the horizon.
That was a splendid sight for the man.
But the little crab thought it not beautiful at all; never yet had he looked so far.
With both his little black eyes he looked at the jellyfish—that was a lovely sight!
Nor did he notice the man who sat there; he was too large for him to perceive.
- 'Will the water come soon?' asked the seaweed; 'we are drying—we shall die.'
- 'The water always comes,' said the little crab in passing—and lifting his flat body high on his six legs,
he followed his path sedately—slantwise toward the jellyfish.
- 'But the water does not come,' sighed the seaweed; 'it takes so long—it has never taken so long.'
- 'Foolish doubters,' said the little crab.
'You vex me.
Would you still live if the water once stayed away?
Who has cared for you, for you and your kind, for all the weed that grows on the stones?
Would you be ungrateful to the water that always returns just when you are nearly dead?
Would the great water that makes us live, that has fed and moistened us,
now let its children perish in drought and misery?
Foolish weed!
you are too small to understand the great justice of the water.
It knows our needs and knows our distress; it gives us moisture when we suffocate and brings food to our mouths.
Ask the mussels—they sit quietly on the stones and do not stir.
Yet when the shells open, the food streams in that the water has chosen for them.
For the water is good and does not stray from its course,
- the water is just and gives each one what is his own.
Shame upon the ungrateful who do not trust!'
The little crab had stood still right before the jellyfish during his long speech.
And after he had finished speaking, he settled on the tastiest spot he had already chosen while talking.
Then he grasped a morsel firmly with his strong pincers,
drew it toward him and began to eat it with his small, nimble jaws.
Calmly and contentedly—for he was the only crab in the neighbourhood and he did not see the man.
The seaweed fell silent in shame—and the little crab went on feasting greedily,
grateful to the great water that had laid his food before him.
Then the man looked up from his reverie, for the sun at the horizon had vanished behind the clouds,
slowly sunk like a great drop of flowing fire.
And the man looked before him between the stones and saw the little crab at his savoury meal.
For a while he watched attentively, drawing nearer and nearer.
But the little crab did not see him.
Then the man made a strange sound.
'Brrr!'
said he, 'how nasty!'
And before the little crab understood what was happening,
his midday meal suddenly flew from his pincers and plopped a good way off into the sea.
Had he not let go in time, he would have been flung along with it.
Now he opened his indignant pincers in furious astonishment and anger and looked to see who had played him that trick.
'Who did that,' said the little crab, 'that is unjust.
It was my food.'
A long flesh-coloured object came close to his claws.
It was a human hand, but unhappily the little crab did not know that.
'Did you do that?
Wait for you!'
said he, 'I shall teach you,' and fiercely he snapped the sharp pincers shut.
That served him ill; he flew farther even than his dead jellyfish—but not toward the sea,
but into the soft, dry sand, far from the waves.
He came down flat on his back and lay a moment stunned.
Then with much effort he managed to turn himself over and stand on his legs again.
He looked wretched, for his moist little body and long legs were covered with thousands of dry grains of sand.
What was he to do.
'Is that just!'
asked the little crab.
'Is that just?
Where is the sea?
- I want to know whether that is just.
It was my food.
The sea shall give me justice.
- Where is the sea?
If only I knew where the sea was!
- I want my rights,' said the little crab.
Hastily he began to run.
One two, one two—slantwise, with high floating steps.
'Where is the sea!
he asked, where is the sea.'
But the shells around him were dead and dry, bleached white by the sun, and gave no answer.
Fortunately the sand grew moister.
The sea was nearer.
A dying little fish lay on the shore.
'Take me to the sea,' it said, 'I am a young herring—and on the point of dying.'
'How can I help it?' said the little crab crossly; 'I have enough to do myself.
I seek justice.'
A little farther off stood a gull close to the waves.
Attentively he stood watching whether the sea would wash anything tasty ashore,
- no little fish or worm escaped his sharp eyes,
'That one will help me,' thought the crab, and from afar he cried: Justice, justice!
- I seek the sea and justice.
They robbed me of my food and threw me on the shore.
The sea shall give me justice.'
The gull turned his swift neck—and looked with one eye at the little crab scurrying nearer.
Silently he waited until it was close, keenly following its movement.
'Justice!'
cried the little crab, 'my food.'
Slantwise he walked straight toward the gull.
The gull said nothing and let him come right up.
And then snap!
- the sharp beak bored through the back of the little crab.
'Justice!'
it still cried—and the next moment it lay flat on the ground—and
the gull drew the entrails from the cloven body.
The sea had risen and covered the black stones wholly with curling, foaming waves.
The patient mussels opened their shells, and let
the cleansing water flow in—the slender seaweed lifted itself in the flood and the supple foliage swayed and waved in the fresh, tumbling water.
'See!
see!'
- they said softly, 'we have been wicked.
Has not the good water come to refresh us?
Yes, the little crab was right; the water is just and remembers its children.'
But on the dry beach lay the picked-clean shell of the little crab, between the outspread legs.
And the wind dried it in the days that followed and the sun bleached it white,
whiter than the foam of the rolling waves.
